ican.text: I can define a radian using the ratio of arc length to radius.
I can convert between degrees and radians, using exact multiples of $\pi$ where appropriate.
I can calculate an arc length or sector area from an angle in radians.
I can rearrange the radian formulas to find an unknown angle or radius.
I can solve problems involving a sector or an annular sector and distinguish its arc lengths, area and perimeter.

ku.text: One radian is the central angle subtending an arc whose length equals the radius. More generally, for arc length $s$ and radius $r>0$, the numerical radian measure is $\theta=s/r$.
A full revolution has arc length $2\pi r$, giving $2\pi$ radians. Therefore $180^\circ=\pi$ radians and $360^\circ=2\pi$ radians.
To convert degrees to radians multiply by $\pi/180$. To convert radians to degrees multiply by $180/\pi$. For example, $150^\circ=5\pi/6$ radians and $3\pi/4$ radians $=135^\circ$.

For a sector of radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$ measured in radians, arc length is $s=r\theta$ and area is $A=\frac12r^2\theta$. These come from multiplying the full circumference and area by the fraction $\theta/(2\pi)$.
The radian formulas require the numerical radian measure, not a degree value. If an angle is given in degrees, convert it first or use the degree formulas from SL 3.4.

The full perimeter of an ordinary sector is $2r+r\theta$. Arc length refers only to the curved part. For an annular sector with outer radius $R$, inner radius $r$ and $0<r<R$, area is $\frac12(R^2-r^2)\theta$ and full perimeter is $R\theta+r\theta+2(R-r)$.
For an ordinary sector with known arc $s$ and angle $\theta>0$, $r=s/\theta$. If radius and area are known, $\theta=2A/r^2$. The angle is in radians in these rearrangements.
Arc lengths are measured in length units and sector areas in square units. Keep exact multiples of $\pi$ until the final approximation. Check angle mode before evaluating trigonometric functions.
Radian measure is dimensionless because $s/r$ is a ratio of lengths. The symbol rad remains useful to make the intended angular measure explicit.

misc.better: A full revolution is $2\pi$ radians; a half-turn is $\pi$ radians.

misc.weak: Use $s=r\theta$ with $\theta=150$ for an angle of $150^\circ$.

misc.better: The correct formula is $A=\frac12r^2\theta$, with $\theta$ in radians.

misc.weak: The perimeter of an annular sector is only its outer arc.
misc.better: Include both arcs and the two straight radial sides.

misc.weak: Multiply radians by $\pi/180$ to get degrees.
misc.better: Multiply radians by $180/\pi$ to get degrees.

terms.text: An angle unit based on arc length divided by radius. One radian subtends an arc equal in length to its radius.
An angle whose vertex is at the centre of a circle.
A region between two concentric circular arcs and two radial line segments.
A value such as $5\pi/6$ that retains $\pi$ rather than replacing it with a rounded decimal.

formula.text: Conversion: $180^\circ=\pi\text{ rad}$; multiply degrees by $\pi/180$ to obtain radians.
For concentric radii $R>r>0$, annular-sector area is $\frac12(R^2-r^2)\theta$.

worked.prompt: A decorative path is an annular sector between two concentric circles of radii $8$ m and $3$ m. Its central angle is $5\pi/6$ radians. Both straight radial sides are included in the boundary.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Convert the central angle to degrees.
parts.a: $\frac{5\pi}{6}\times\frac{180}{\pi}=150^\circ$. The angle is between a quarter-turn and a half-turn, which is consistent.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find the exact lengths of the outer and inner arcs.
parts.a: Use $s=r\theta$. The outer arc is $8(5\pi/6)=20\pi/3$ m; the inner arc is $3(5\pi/6)=5\pi/2$ m.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Find the exact area of the path and its area to three significant figures.
parts.a: Subtract the inner sector from the outer sector: $A=\frac12(8^2-3^2)(5\pi/6)=275\pi/12\text{ m}^2\approx72.0\text{ m}^2$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Find the exact total perimeter of the path.
parts.a: Add both arcs and the two radial sides, each of length $8-3=5$ m: $P=20\pi/3+5\pi/2+10=55\pi/6+10$ m.

parts.label: e
parts.q: A different sector has radius $8$ m and arc length $12$ m. Find its angle in radians and its area.

kq.q: Why is a complete turn $2\pi$ radians?
kq.model: The circumference is $2\pi r$, so the ratio of the full arc length to the radius is $2\pi r/r=2\pi$.
Radian measure is defined by $\theta=s/r$. Rearranging gives $s=r\theta$ directly; a degree measure needs a conversion factor.

kq.q: Why is the annular-sector area a difference?
kq.model: The path is the outer sector with the smaller, concentric sector removed. Both sectors have the same central angle.

kq.q: When do calculator angle settings matter?
kq.model: They matter when evaluating a trigonometric function or inverse function unless the calculator entry explicitly specifies an angle unit. Check the setting for the measurement in the question.
